The graph is complete:

```
contract  →  { implement-typescript , implement-python }  →  conformance-review
                                        ↑______feedback______|   (both clients)
```

- **contract** — writes `contracts/retry-policy.md` first, after inspecting both SDK clients, and pins the open choices (delay values, jitter, default max attempts, idempotence signal) so both implementations share one binding definition.
- **implement-typescript / implement-python** — run in parallel once the contract exists; each edits only its own client plus its unit tests, implements every policy clause (429/503 retry set, Retry-After both forms, backoff formula/cap, attempt limit and override, non-idempotent protection, exhaustion error), and is explicitly barred from touching the server or browser app.
- **conformance-review** — depends on both, and empirically compares them clause by clause in `tests/sdk-conformance.md`: reproducible scenarios with stubbed clock/transport, recorded per-client results, a comparison table and a verdict on semantic identity. Any divergence or contract deviation triggers bounded feedback to the affected client implementations, which then forces a repeat conformance review.

Deliberate planning choices worth flagging: open policy values are resolved once by the contract owner rather than preselected downstream; implementation and its unit tests stay in one node per client to avoid two owners of the same file; and the correction loop targets only the clients, since you scoped fixes to the implementations and left `contracts/retry-policy.md` read-only to them.
